expectedText:
DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP DECLARATION
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

RECITALS — PARTIES AND BASIS
This Domestic Partnership Declaration is made by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee (together, "the Partners") in connection with their registration, or intended registration, as domestic partners. This document is intended to record facts and statutory citations relevant to that registration; it does not itself constitute the statutory filing, which is made on the form prescribed by the applicable filing authority.

ELIGIBILITY TO REGISTER AS DOMESTIC PARTNERS
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, as of September 1, 2026, each of the following is true: neither is married to another person or a partner in another domestic partnership that has not been terminated, dissolved, or adjudged a nullity; the two are not related by blood in a way that would prevent marriage to each other in California; each is at least 18 years of age; and each is capable of consenting to a domestic partnership.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Domestic partners are two adults who have chosen to share one another's lives in an intimate and committed relationship of mutual caring. (b) A domestic partnership shall be established in California when both persons file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this division, and, at the time of filing, all of the following requirements are met: (1) Neither person is married to someone else or is a member of another domestic partnership with someone else that has not been terminated, dissolved, or adjudged a nullity. (2) The two persons are not related by blood in a way that would prevent them from being married to each other in this state. (3) Both persons are at least 18 years of age, except as provided in Section 297.1. (4) Both persons are capable of consenting to the domestic partnership."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the current eligibility requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what "domestic partnership" eligibility can require — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific couple's registration, or that these are the only requirements anywhere. Domestic partnership and civil union status varies enormously by state, and many states have no such status at all now that marriage is available nationally regardless of sex. This is a single statutory section (§ 297); no additional independent source was found for this.

HOW A DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP IS REGISTERED
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that a domestic partnership is established by filing a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the California Secretary of State, and that the Declaration form requires each person to state that they meet the statutory eligibility requirements, provide a mailing address, consent to the jurisdiction of the California Superior Courts for a future dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation proceeding, and sign under penalty of the form's declaration that all statements are true and complete, with the signature notarized. The Secretary of State registers the filed Declaration and returns a Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership to the partners.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The Declaration of Domestic Partnership shall require each person who wants to become a domestic partner to (1) state that the person meets the requirements of Section 297 at the time the form is signed, (2) provide a mailing address, (3) state that the person consents to the jurisdiction of the Superior Courts of California for the purpose of a proceeding to obtain a judgment of dissolution or nullity of the domestic partnership or for legal separation of partners in the domestic partnership, or for any other proceeding related to the partners' rights and obligations, even if one or both partners ceases to be a resident of, or to maintain a domicile in, this state, (4) sign the form with a declaration that representations made therein are true, correct, and contain no material omissions of fact to the best knowledge and belief of the applicant, and (5) have a notary public acknowledge the signature. Both partners' signatures shall be affixed to one Declaration of Domestic Partnership form, which shall then be transmitted to the Secretary of State according to the instructions provided on the form. Filing an intentionally and materially false Declaration of Domestic Partnership shall be punishable as a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 298(c) (California Legislative Information text), required Declaration form content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=298.)
  "(a) Two persons desiring to become domestic partners may complete and file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State. (b) The Secretary of State shall register the Declaration of Domestic Partnership in a registry for those partnerships, and shall return a copy of the registered form, a Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership, and a copy of the brochure ... to the domestic partners at the mailing address provided by the domestic partners."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 298.5(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), filing and registration by the Secretary of State (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=298.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's filing mechanism, used as real evidence of how a registration-based partnership status can be created — not a claim about which state's procedure applies to a specific couple, or that every jurisdiction with a similar status uses this same mechanism. Registration procedures, required disclosures, and notarization rules vary by state.

STATUTORY EFFECT OF REGISTRATION — SAME RIGHTS AND DUTIES AS SPOUSES
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under California law, registered domestic partners have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law — whether arising from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other source of law — as are granted to and imposed upon spouses, including with respect to any child of either partner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon spouses. ... (d) The rights and obligations of registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of spouses."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text), the same-rights-and-duties statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a domestic partnership can carry marriage-equivalent legal consequences under that state's law — not a claim about the legal effect of a specific domestic partnership in any other state or under federal law generally. Whether a domestic partnership registered in one state produces marriage-equivalent rights in another state, or is recognized at all, is not addressed by this statute. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(a), (d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY AND MARITAL PROPERTY STATUTES APPLY
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, for purposes of the community property statutes, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, spousal-support rights on dissolution, and other property statutes that turn on the date of a marriage, California law treats the date of registration of the domestic partnership as the reference date, in the same way the date of marriage functions for spouses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "For purposes of the statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, and any other provision or source of law governing the rights, protections, and benefits, and the responsibilities, obligations, and duties of registered domestic partners in this state, as effectuated by this section, with respect to community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, the right in particular circumstances of either partner to seek financial support from the other following the dissolution of the partnership, and other rights and duties as between the partners concerning ownership of property, any reference to the date of a marriage shall be deemed to refer to the date of registration of a domestic partnership with the state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the registration date functions as the marriage-date reference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(k)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a domestic partnership status can be tied to community-property rules by law — not a claim about which state's property regime, if any, applies to a specific couple's property. Community property is itself a minority regime among U.S. states, and a domestic partnership registered elsewhere may carry no property consequences at all.

CONFIDENTIAL DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP CATEGORY
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that California law separately provides for a confidential domestic partnership: two people who have been living together as domestic partners and who meet the substantive eligibility requirements may enter a confidential Declaration of Domestic Partnership, which the Secretary of State maintains as a permanent record not open to public inspection except by court order on a showing of good cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The Secretary of State shall establish a process by which two persons, who have been living together as domestic partners and who meet the requirements of paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (b) of Section 297, may enter into a confidential domestic partnership. This process shall do all of the following: (a) Maintain each confidential Declaration of Domestic Partnership as a permanent record that is not open to public inspection except upon order of the court issued upon a showing of good cause. (b) Authorize the Secretary of State to charge a reasonable fee to offset costs directly connected with maintaining confidentiality of a Declaration of Domestic Partnership."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 298.7 (California Legislative Information text), the confidential domestic partnership process (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=298.7.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 298.7); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential, non-public filing track for a registration-based partnership status can exist alongside the standard public filing — not a claim about whether any other state offers a comparable confidential category, or that this California category applies outside California. Confidential marriage and confidential-partnership categories are not universal among states.

DECLARATION OF INTENT TO REGISTER
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee declare that they intend to become registered domestic partners and, on or about September 1, 2026, intend to complete and file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the office of the California Secretary of State, or with the corresponding filing authority of the state in which they register.

ENDING A DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP — ADMINISTRATIVE NOTICE VS. COURT DISSOLUTION
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that California law provides two distinct paths to end a registered domestic partnership. A simplified administrative path — filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State without a court proceeding — is available only if, at the time of filing, both partners sign the Notice; there are no children of the relationship (born, adopted, or on the way) common to the partners; the partnership is not more than five years in duration; neither partner has any interest in real property (with a narrow exception for a short-term residential lease without a purchase option); neither partner has unpaid obligations or community-property assets above the statutory thresholds tied to Family Code § 2400; the partners have executed an agreement dividing their assets and liabilities; both partners waive any right to support from the other; both have read the Secretary of State's brochure on terminating a domestic partnership; and both desire termination. Absent those conditions, ending a partnership requires a dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation proceeding in California Superior Court, following the same procedures and producing the same rights, protections, benefits, responsibilities, obligations, and duties as apply to the dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A registered domestic partnership may be terminated without filing a proceeding for dissolution of domestic partnership by the filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that all of the following conditions exist at the time of the filing: (1) The Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership is signed by both registered domestic partners. (2) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or after registration of the domestic partnership or adopted by the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, and neither of the registered domestic partners, to their knowledge, is pregnant. (3) The registered domestic partnership is not more than five years in duration. (4) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership. (5) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of the amount described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, incurred by either or both of the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (6) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than the amount described in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of that amount. (7) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community property, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (8) The parties waive any rights to support by the other domestic partner. (9) The parties have read and understand a brochure prepared by the Secretary of State describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership. (10) Both parties desire that the domestic partnership be terminated. ... (d) The superior courts shall have jurisdiction over all proceedings relating to the dissolution of domestic partnerships, nullity of domestic partnerships, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership. The dissolution of a domestic partnership, nullity of a domestic partnership, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership shall follow the same procedures, and the partners shall possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply to the dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, and legal separation of spouses in a marriage, respectively, except as provided in subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text), administrative termination conditions and court dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a registration-based partnership status can be terminated administratively versus judicially — not a claim about which state's procedure, if any, applies to a specific termination, nor a claim about the current dollar thresholds referenced in Family Code § 2400 (which are indexed and change over time and were not independently verified here). Many states have no simplified administrative termination procedure for any relationship status. This is a single statutory section (§ 299); no additional independent source was found for this.

EFFECT OF THE SAME PARTNERS LATER MARRYING EACH OTHER
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that California law does not treat a subsequent marriage between the same two registered domestic partners as automatically terminating or merging into the domestic partnership; instead, partners who are also married to one another may petition the court to dissolve both the domestic partnership and the marriage together, in a single proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Parties to a registered domestic partnership who are also married to one another may petition the court to dissolve both their domestic partnership and their marriage in a single proceeding, in a form that shall be prescribed by the Judicial Council."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(e) (California Legislative Information text), combined dissolution petition for a married domestic-partner couple (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(e)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction sequences a domestic partnership and a later marriage between the same two people — not a claim about how another state, if different, would treat that sequence. Some states that recognize domestic partnerships or civil unions have adopted automatic-merger or automatic-termination rules instead; this statute does not describe those.

RECOGNITION OF EQUIVALENT OUT-OF-STATE LEGAL UNIONS
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that California law recognizes, as a valid California domestic partnership, a legal union of two people — other than a marriage — that was validly formed in another jurisdiction and is substantially equivalent to a California domestic partnership, regardless of what name that other jurisdiction gives it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A legal union of two persons, other than a marriage, that was validly formed in another jurisdiction, and that is substantially equivalent to a domestic partnership as defined in this part, shall be recognized as a valid domestic partnership in this state regardless of whether it bears the name domestic partnership."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299.2 (California Legislative Information text), recognition of an equivalent out-of-state union (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.2.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 299.2); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state can choose to recognize an out-of-state, non-marital legal union as equivalent to its own domestic partnership status — not a claim about whether any specific out-of-state union meets California's "substantially equivalent" standard, or about how any other state (if different from California) treats an out-of-state civil union or domestic partnership. Recognition rules for non-marital relationship statuses vary widely, and many states have no equivalent status to recognize at all.

BAR ON A NEW FILING OR MARRIAGE WHILE A PRIOR PARTNERSHIP IS UNRESOLVED
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under California law, a person who has already filed a Declaration of Domestic Partnership may not file a new one, or enter a civil marriage with someone other than their registered partner, unless the most recent domestic partnership has been terminated or a final judgment of its dissolution or nullity has been entered — except that this bar does not apply if the prior partnership ended because a partner died.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A person who has filed a Declaration of Domestic Partnership may not file a new Declaration of Domestic Partnership or enter a civil marriage with someone other than their registered domestic partner unless the most recent domestic partnership has been terminated or a final judgment of dissolution or nullity of the most recent domestic partnership has been entered. This prohibition does not apply if the previous domestic partnership ended because one of the partners died."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 298.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), the exclusivity bar on a new filing or marriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=298.5.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 298.5(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a registration-based partnership status can carry an exclusivity requirement enforced at the point of a later filing — not a claim about whether any other state imposes an equivalent bar.

SIGNATURES AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee have executed this Domestic Partnership Declaration on September 1, 2026.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment block, if required by the filing jurisdiction, follows on a separate page.
